chapter.name: Proportional Reasoning-1
chapter.blurb: Ratios and proportional change; testing whether two ratios are proportional and writing this with the a : b :: c : d notation; the cross multiplication rule ad = bc and Aryabhata's Rule of Three (Trairasika); solving proportion word problems while keeping units consistent and recognising when a situation is not a direct proportion; dividing a quantity into parts in a given ratio; and unit conversions for length, area, volume and temperature used alongside ratio reasoning.

scope_in.item: Compare two rectangular or square images and recognise that images whose width and height change by the same multiplying factor look similar, while ones that change by a fixed difference, or by a different factor, look distorted

State that a change is called proportional when two quantities change by the same factor through multiplication, and that changing both by the same amount through addition or subtraction is not the same thing
Read a ratio a : b as 'for every a units of the first quantity there are b units of the second', and identify the two terms of a ratio
Reduce a ratio to its simplest form by dividing both terms by their HCF
Test whether two given ratios are proportional by checking whether they are equal in simplest form, and write this using the notation a : b :: c : d
State that adding or subtracting the same number from both terms of a ratio does not, in general, give a ratio proportional to the original one, unlike multiplying both terms by the same factor
Given three terms of a proportion a : b :: c : d, find the fourth by identifying the multiplying factor between two corresponding terms
Derive that a : b :: c : d implies ad = bc, starting from c = fa and d = fb, and use this cross multiplication rule to find an unknown term of a proportion

State the Rule of Three (Trairasika) as given by Aryabhata, using the terms pramana (measure), phala (fruit) and ichchha (requisition) to find the ichchhaphala (yield), and connect it to the cross multiplication rule
Recognise that both ratios in a proportion must use the same units before they are set up as a : b :: c : d, and convert units where needed before solving
Judge, with a reason, whether a given real-world situation can or cannot be modelled as a direct proportion using the Rule of Three, such as why travel time is not directly proportional to speed

Divide a given quantity x into two parts in a given ratio m : n by splitting it into m + n equal groups, and state the general formulas (m times x) / (m + n) and (n times x) / (m + n) for the two parts

Apply the ratio-division method to word problems on sharing a profit or an amount of money in a given ratio, including finding how much of one ingredient must be added to change an existing mixture ratio to a new target ratio

Convert between units of length (metre to feet), area (square metre to square feet, acre, hectare) and volume (millilitre, cubic centimetre, litre) using the conversion facts given in the chapter's reference table
Convert temperature between Celsius and Fahrenheit using Fahrenheit = (9/5) times Celsius + 32 and Celsius = (5/9) times (Fahrenheit - 32)

Solve a word problem that combines a given ratio with a required unit conversion, such as a land cost per acre converted to a smaller area in square feet, or a manure rate per acre applied to a plot measured in feet

scope_out.item: Inverse proportion or inverse variation solved as a named, worked method (e.g. finding how time decreases as speed increases)
scope_out.reason: The chapter raises this only as a warning, through Puneeth's father's speed and travel time on p. 171, that the Rule of Three does not apply; no method for solving an inverse-proportion problem is taught

scope_out.item: Percentages, and converting a ratio into a percentage
scope_out.reason: Percentages are not mentioned anywhere in this chapter

scope_out.item: Compound or three-term ratios (a : b : c) and problems that combine more than two quantities into one ratio
scope_out.reason: Every ratio and proportion in the chapter has exactly two terms; three-term ratios such as sand : cement : water are never used

scope_out.item: Speed, distance and time as a topic in its own right, or the formula speed = distance / time
scope_out.reason: km/h appears only inside the Puneeth's father counter-example on p. 171 precisely to show that proportion does NOT apply there; no speed-distance-time formula is taught or used to solve a problem

scope_out.item: Direct and inverse variation written as algebraic functions (y = kx or y = k/x), graphs of proportional relationships, or a named constant of proportionality k
scope_out.reason: The chapter's algebra stops at deriving ad = bc; no function notation or graph of a proportional relationship is used

scope_out.item: Simple interest, compound interest, or profit-and-loss expressed as a percentage
scope_out.reason: Example 11 only splits a given rupee profit in a given ratio between two partners; no percentage profit, loss or interest formula appears

scope_out.item: Similar triangles or a formal geometric similarity criterion (AA, SSS, SAS similarity)
scope_out.reason: The opening idea of images 'looking similar' on pp. 159-160 is an informal comparison of proportional width and height, not a geometric theorem about triangles

scope_out.item: A separately named 'unitary method' presented as a distinct step-by-step procedure from the Rule of Three
scope_out.reason: The chapter presents finding a common multiplying factor and cross multiplication as its two solving strategies; it never names or teaches a separate unitary method procedure

scope_out.item: The Binairo logic puzzle and the Dot Grid activity pages
scope_out.reason: These are a stand-alone logic game and blank drawing grids on pp. 178-180 with no ratio or proportion content of their own to be tested

concepts.name: Ratios: meaning, terms and simplest form
concepts.description: Reading a ratio, identifying its terms, and reducing it to simplest form using the HCF.
concepts.idea: A ratio compares two quantities by division, and reducing it to simplest form makes it easy to compare with another ratio.
concepts.rule: A ratio a : b means for every a units of the first quantity there are b units of the second; a and b are its terms. Dividing both terms by their HCF gives the simplest form.
concepts.example: The ratio 60 : 40 has HCF 20, so in simplest form it is 3 : 2.

But the student's claim about adding 2 to every term is wrong: 10 : 5 simplifies to 2 : 1, while 26 : 11 does not simplify to 2 : 1 (its simplest form is 26 : 11 itself, since its HCF is 1), so the two new ratios are not proportional. concepts.name: Cross multiplication and the Rule of Three
concepts.description: Deriving a x d = b x c from a proportion a : b :: c : d, and Aryabhata's Rule of Three using pramana, phala, ichchha and ichchhaphala.
concepts.idea: Writing a proportion as a : b :: c : d and cross multiplying its terms turns it into a simple equation that can be solved for an unknown.
concepts.rule: If a : b :: c : d, then a multiplied by d equals b multiplied by c (cross multiplication). Aryabhata's Rule of Three uses pramana (measure, a), phala (fruit, b) and ichchha (requisition, c) to find the ichchhaphala (yield, d), equal to (phala times ichchha) divided by pramana.
concepts.example: For a mid-day meal, 120 students need 15 kg of rice; for 80 students, 120 : 15 :: 80 : d gives d = (15 x 80) / 120 = 10 kg.

concepts.name: Solving proportion problems: unit consistency and when direct proportion applies
concepts.description: Converting quantities to the same unit before setting up a proportion, and judging whether a real situation is a direct proportion at all.
concepts.idea: Before setting up a proportion, both ratios must compare quantities in the same unit; and not every real situation changes proportionally, since some quantities decrease as others increase.
concepts.rule: Convert all quantities to the same unit before writing a : b :: c : d, and check first whether the two quantities actually increase and decrease together before using a direct proportion.
concepts.example: A car's distance-time proportion needs 4 hours converted to 240 minutes before it can be set up as 150 : 90 :: 240 : d; but travel time and speed do not work this way, since a higher speed gives a shorter time, not a longer one.

concepts.name: Dividing a quantity in a given ratio
concepts.description: Splitting a whole into two parts in a given ratio by dividing it into equal groups, and the general formula for each part.
concepts.idea: To divide a quantity x in the ratio m : n, split x into m + n equal groups and give m groups to one share and n groups to the other.
concepts.rule: Dividing x in the ratio m : n gives parts (m times x) / (m + n) and (n times x) / (m + n).
concepts.example: Dividing 12 in the ratio 3 : 1 gives parts 9 and 3, since 12 / (3 + 1) = 3 per group, 3 groups is 9 and 1 group is 3.
